text: Adolescents’ development occurs within interconnected systems that can both facilitate and constrain growth. Family and school serve as key immediate contexts, and their interrelations form part of the mesosystem through which adolescents receive socialization [ 4 ]. In the developmental assets framework, these contextual resources are conceptualized as external assets that foster positive development [ 2 , 17 , 27 ]. Positive development is generally conceptualized as a multidimensional construct that includes competencies, strengths, adaptive functioning, and well-being [ 41 ]. In the present study, adolescents’ positive development was represented by three theoretically distinct domains: reading competence, resilience, and positive feelings. Reading competence reflects achievement-related functioning; resilience captures adaptive capacity in response to stress and environmental demands; and positive feelings represent adolescents’ positive subjective experiences. Together, these indicators capture complementary facets of positive development, spanning achievement-related functioning, adaptive capacity, and subjective well-being.
source_label: Cultural comparison of positive development: network analyses of adolescents’ ecological systems in Mainland and non-Mainland China
